lessons.title: Run an isolated R script
lessons.summary: Change Ready to Changed, save, and run the same Rscript command again. Which message is produced?
explanation: Save the example as main.R and run Rscript --vanilla main.R. --vanilla avoids saved-workspace restoration and startup-profile customization; it does not install packages or make every external dependency identical.
cat writes supplied values as text. The string "\n" supplies a newline; print instead produces an R-style representation that can include index labels such as [1].

These fixtures run on R 4.5.0 with available base packages. Current official release manuals describe a newer release; this course does not claim the installed runtime is the latest version. The app is a concept reader, not an R browser runner.

Complete local R example; the app itself does not execute it:
```r
cat("Ready", "\n", sep="")
```

lessons.title: Atomic vectors and coercion
lessons.summary: Replace the second value with "two". What type is reported?
explanation: c(1, 2) combines values into an atomic vector. Its elements share a common storage type; c is a function call, not a declaration of separate scalar variables.
Combining numeric values with text converts this atomic vector to character data. Logical values can be converted to numbers when combined with numeric values.
typeof(values) returns the storage type name. This is distinct from class, which can describe higher-level behavior such as a factor or data frame.

Complete local R example; the app itself does not execute it:
```r
values <- c(1, 2)
cat(typeof(values))
```
Expected output or behavior: double. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

lessons.title: Integer double and finite precision
lessons.summary: Remove L from 1L. What type prints?
explanation: 1 is normally a double-precision numeric value in R, even though it looks like a whole number.
1L creates an integer value. typeof distinguishes integer from double; both can participate in numeric calculations.
Double precision cannot represent every real number exactly. Integer storage has a finite range; neither type is an unlimited exact arithmetic guarantee.

```r

cat(typeof(value))
```

lessons.title: Vector arithmetic and recycling
lessons.summary: Replace c(10,20) with the single value 10. What prints?
explanation: For equal-length numeric vectors, + adds corresponding positions rather than concatenating them.
c(1,2,3,4) + c(10,20) repeats the shorter vector to match four positions. A non-multiple length can warn; a warning is not a validation policy.
Adding 10 to this vector adds ten to every entry. For unrelated data, check lengths explicitly instead of relying on accidental recycling.
cat(result, sep=",") prints entries separated by commas. sep controls formatting, not the calculation.

Complete local R example; the app itself does not execute it:
```r
values <- c(1, 2, 3, 4)
cat(values + c(10, 20), sep=",")
```
Expected output or behavior: 11,22,13,24. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

lessons.title: Logical vectors and scalar conditions
lessons.summary: Replace the right operand TRUE with FALSE. What prints?
explanation: c(TRUE,FALSE) is a two-element logical vector. NA can represent an unknown logical value.
& and | operate elementwise. && and || are short-circuit operators for scalar conditions; supplying a vector longer than one is an error in this tested runtime.

if needs one non-missing logical result. A scalar numeric value can be coerced to logical, but explicit comparisons make intent clearer. It does not choose a policy for an entire vector or an unknown value.

```r
flags <- c(TRUE, FALSE)
cat(flags & TRUE, sep=",")
```

A subscript vector containing both a positive and a negative nonzero index is rejected. Choose either selection or omission consistently.

lessons.title: Logical indexing with missing values
lessons.summary: Add the explicit !is.na(values) & check to the mask. What prints?
explanation: A mask from values > 2 selects elements whose comparison is TRUE. A comparison involving NA normally produces NA.
Indexing an atomic vector with an NA mask entry includes a missing result at that position. Unknown does not silently mean false.

is.na(values) marks missing entries. ! negates those flags. Combining !is.na(values) & (values > 2) rejects missing entries while retaining known qualifying values. Both masks are evaluated elementwise: & is not short-circuiting, and FALSE & NA is FALSE.

Complete local R example; the app itself does not execute it:
```r
values <- c(1, NA, 4)
cat(values[values > 2], sep=",")
```

lessons.title: NA NaN and infinite values
lessons.summary: Replace is.na with is.finite. What prints?
explanation: NA represents missing information. NaN represents an undefined numeric result. Inf and -Inf represent positive and negative infinity.
is.na is TRUE for NA and NaN, but FALSE for Inf and ordinary finite values. Comparing a value with NA does not establish whether it is missing.
is.finite is TRUE only for finite numeric values, so it is FALSE for NA, NaN and infinities.

lessons.title: Dimensions and drop false
lessons.summary: Remove drop=FALSE. What class prints for this numeric column?
explanation: Selecting one data-frame column with frame[, "score"] normally simplifies to the underlying vector.
frame[, "score", drop=FALSE] keeps a one-column data frame. The values are the same, but the container shape differs.
A function expecting row/column structure can behave differently when given a vector. Do not infer shape only from the printed numbers.

Complete local R example; the app itself does not execute it:
```r
frame <- data.frame(score=c(2, 4))
selected <- frame[, "score", drop=FALSE]
```

lessons.title: Factors labels and integer codes
lessons.summary: Convert to character before numeric: as.numeric(as.character(value)). What prints for these labels?

lessons.title: Matrices and array ordering
lessons.summary: Add byrow=TRUE when creating the matrix. What prints?
explanation: matrix(c(1,2,3,4), nrow=2) creates a two-row matrix. An array generalizes dimensions beyond rows and columns.
With byrow=FALSE, the first column receives 1 and 2, then the second receives 3 and 4. byrow=TRUE fills rows instead.
m[1,2] reads row 1, column 2. Changing the fill order changes where input values are placed, not the meaning of the two indices.

lessons.title: For loops and safe sequences
lessons.summary: Replace values with numeric(0). What prints?
explanation: for (index in seq_along(values)) visits each valid position of this vector. It does not require a separate manual counter update.
seq_along(numeric(0)) is an empty index sequence. The colon operator makes a sequence including both endpoints. Thus 1:length(values) becomes 1:0 for empty input, which is not an empty sequence.
numeric(length(values)) can allocate a result vector before a loop. Avoid repeatedly growing large vectors without measuring the cost.
count <- count + 1 updates the local count once per iteration. The starting zero remains zero if the sequence is empty.

Complete local R example; the app itself does not execute it:
```r
values <- c(2, 4)
count <- 0
for (index in seq_along(values)) {
  count <- count + 1
}
cat(count)
```

lessons.title: Function results defaults and named arguments
lessons.summary: Supply offset=-1 as an additional named argument. What prints?
explanation: function(score, offset=1) declares a required score and a default offset. Named arguments can be supplied explicitly rather than relying on position.
The last evaluated expression supplies the result unless return exits earlier. Returning a value is distinct from printing it.
R supports several argument-matching rules, including partial matching in some situations. Exact names are clearer and less vulnerable to future parameter additions.

lessons.title: Lexical lookup and local assignment
lessons.summary: Remove the inner value <- 9 assignment. What prints?
explanation: A function can read a value from the environment where it was created when no local binding shadows it. This is lexical lookup, not a search through every caller’s local variables.
value <- 9 in this function does not automatically overwrite the outer value. The super-assignment operator <<- has different effects and is not used here.
The function returns its final local value. cat prints that result followed by the outer value, separated by a comma.

Complete local R example; the app itself does not execute it:
```r
value <- 2
shown <- function() {
  value <- 9
  value
}
cat(shown(), value, sep=",")
```
Expected output or behavior: 9,2. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.
